passage:
Monday: In class, Asha Ma'am teaches a new phrase: 'Atithi devo bhava. A guest is like God.' Wasim, five, chants it all the way home.
Wednesday: Khala comes to visit. Before Ammi Farida can ask, Wasim carries Khala a steel glass of water in both hands, spilling a little. Khala kisses his head.
Friday: More guests. Ammi puts out the last three kebabs. Wasim reaches for one, and Ammi shakes her head. 'Guests first, beta.' He pouts, then carries the plate to the uncle himself, watching every bite. Later, in the kitchen, Ammi slips him a kebab she saved.

qa.q: What phrase did Asha Ma'am teach?
qa.a: 'Atithi devo bhava. A guest is like God.'

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when Ammi said 'Guests first, beta'?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a bit sulky, pouting and watching every bite, though he still served the plate.

qa.q: What did Ammi Farida do afterwards that balanced the lesson?
qa.a: She slipped him a saved kebab, showing that serving guests first does not mean his wants don't matter.

qa.q: How might Khala feel when Wasim carries water to her in both hands?
qa.a: Khala likely feels welcomed and touched by his effort, which is why she kisses his head.

grounding: Shows a young child who learns that a guest is like God, offers water and serves food, and also learns that the best portion goes to visitors first.

passage: The guests arrived during a power cut, and there was almost nothing in the kitchen. Mumma Gurleen whispered, 'Raghav, atithi devo bhava, remember? Help me.' By candlelight, six-year-old Raghav counted the laddoos in the tin: five. The guests were four. He carried the plate out carefully, offering it with both hands the way Mumma had shown him, and set the biggest laddoo nearest the old aunty. When the plate came back, one small laddoo was left. He looked at it, then at Mumma. She nodded. He ate it in tiny bites, glowing, as if he'd earned it.

qa.q: How many laddoos were in the tin?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he ate the last laddoo?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, as if the laddoo were a reward for serving the guests well.

qa.q: What helped Raghav serve guests even in the dark with so little food?
qa.a: Mumma gave him a clear job and had already shown him how to offer with both hands, so he felt useful and capable.

qa.q: How might the old aunty feel being offered the biggest laddoo by a small child?
qa.a: She would likely feel honoured and charmed, sensing the care in a child's careful offering.

grounding: Illustrates a young child told that a guest is like God, who serves visitors with care and gives them the best portion first, even when there is little to share.

passage:
"Atithi devo bhava," Nandini ma'am told the class. "A guest is like God. So when the visitors come today, what do we do?"

"Give water!" shouted Vikas, five.

When the two visitors from the education office sat down, Vikas carried a steel glass across the room with both hands, tongue between his teeth. Not one drop spilled.

At snack time there were three laddoos left, one bigger than the others. Vikas looked at it a long time. Then he put the big one on the visitor's plate.

The visitor smiled. "Thank you, beta."

Vikas skipped back, proud and only a little sorry about the laddoo.

qa.q: How many laddoos were left at snack time?
qa.a: There were three laddoos left.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Vikas have after giving away the big laddoo?
qa.a: Vikas felt proud of serving the guest and a little sorry to lose the biggest laddoo.

qa.q: How could Nandini ma'am build on Vikas's kindness?
qa.a: Praise his care and let children take turns serving, so the best portion is given happily rather than as a rule.

qa.q: How might the visitor feel when Vikas gives the big laddoo?
qa.a: The visitor likely feels warmly welcomed and touched by such careful service.

grounding: Shows a young child taught atithi devo bhava who serves water to guests and gives the best sweet to the visitor first.

passage:
Friday: "Your school says atithi devo bhava," Ammi said, folding napkins. "We say a guest brings blessings. Same heart." Farida, five, nodded seriously.

Saturday: Lalremsiami Aunty from the next flat came for tea. Farida carried in the water glass, then the plate of cream biscuits, and set the whole ones in front of Aunty, keeping the broken ones for herself.

Sunday: At lunch the biggest mango slice went to Aunty's plate again. Farida frowned. "Why does Aunty always get the best?"

Ammi laughed. "Because she's our guest. And when you visit her, she'll give you the best."

Farida thought about that, then ran to ask Aunty when she could visit.

qa.q: What did Farida keep for herself?
qa.a: She kept the broken ones for herself.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she asked why Aunty always gets the best?
qa.a: Farida felt a little jealous and puzzled that the best portion always went to the guest.

qa.q: How did Ammi help Farida understand the custom?
qa.a: She explained that hospitality goes both ways, so Farida could see serving the guest as love rather than loss.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami Aunty feel when Farida serves her?
qa.a: Aunty likely feels welcomed and fond of the careful little host.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to serve guests with love, and puzzling over why the best portion goes to the visitor first.

passage:
The power had been out since evening, and there was only half a packet of milk left when the doorbell rang. Deepak Mama, Mami and their two boys, surprise visitors from Gwalior.

Mummy whispered, "Atithi devo bhava, Reena. Help me."

Reena, six, carried the steel water glasses by candlelight, one at a time, very slowly. When Mummy made tea, Reena saw there was no milk left for her own bedtime glass.

She opened her mouth to complain, then looked at the boys yawning on the sofa and closed it.

Deepak Mama noticed. He broke the biggest piece from the box of sweets they had brought and gave it to her. "For our best waiter."

qa.q: How much milk was left when the doorbell rang?
qa.a: There was only half a packet of milk left.

qa.q: Why did Reena close her mouth instead of complaining?
qa.a: She felt disappointed about her milk but caring toward the tired guests, so she let them have it.

qa.q: How could Mummy acknowledge what Reena gave up?
qa.a: Thank her for serving so carefully and admit that giving up her milk was a real sacrifice, perhaps making it up tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Deepak Mama see Reena's service?
qa.a: Deepak Mama notices and appreciates it, giving her the biggest piece of the sweets and calling her the best waiter.

grounding: Shows a young child serving surprise guests by candlelight and accepting that the visitors come first, with her care noticed.

passage: When Ishita aunty came to visit their Indore flat, Dadi said, "Madhav, atithi devo bhava. Guest is like God." Madhav, five, carried a glass of water with both hands. Aunty smiled and said, "Thank you, beta." Then Dadi put the last gulab jamun on aunty's plate. Madhav stared at it. He had wanted it all day. His lip went out a little. Aunty saw. She cut it in half and gave him one piece. Dadi laughed, "See? Serve with love, and love comes back." Madhav ate slowly, happy.

qa.q: What did Dadi put on Ishita aunty's plate?
qa.a: The last gulab jamun.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when the last gulab jamun went to aunty?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, his lip going out a little, because he had wanted it all day.

qa.q: What did Madhav learn from the visit?
qa.a: That serving guests first is a way of showing love, and kindness often comes back.

qa.q: How might Ishita aunty have felt when she saw Madhav's face?
qa.a: She probably felt tender and amused, so she shared half the sweet with him.

grounding: It illustrates a child told atithi devo bhava who serves the guest and learns the best portion goes to the visitor first.
